ELECTIVE AREA 3 · MAY · JUNE

Platonic solids

A cube consists of six equal squares, and three of them meet at every corner. Are there more solids built as regularly as that? There are exactly five, and you can prove why there is no sixth. You build them as models, count their vertices, edges and faces and discover a formula that Leonhard Euler found. And you find out what Plato and Kepler had in mind with these solids.

8 LESSONS2 UNITS2 LABS
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • apply the terms polyhedron and regular polyhedron
  • explain why there are exactly five regular polyhedra
  • build models of the five Platonic solids from nets
  • check and apply Euler’s polyhedron formula $e - k + f = 2$
  • draw some regular polyhedra as oblique drawings

UNIT 14 LESSONS

1The five regular polyhedra

Building shows: three, four or five triangles round a point can be folded together into a pointed corner. Six triangles lie flat on the table; their angles add up to exactly $6 \cdot 60^\circ = 360^\circ$. No corner comes of that. Exactly this observation leads to the proof.

KEY POINT · POLYHEDRA AND REGULAR POLYHEDRA

A polyhedron is a solid bounded only by flat polygons. Prisms and pyramids are polyhedra.

A polyhedron without dents is called regular if all its faces are congruent regular polygons and the same number of faces meet at every corner.

There are exactly five regular polyhedra, the Platonic solids: tetrahedron, cube (hexahedron), octahedron, dodecahedron and icosahedron.

Names: Greek tetra four, hexa six, okta eight, dodeka twelve, eikosi twenty, hedra face.

WHY THERE ARE EXACTLY FIVE
  1. At every corner of a solid at least three faces meet.
  2. The angles of these faces at the corner add up to less than $360^\circ$. At exactly $360^\circ$ they lie flat; above that they overlap.
  3. Triangles ($60^\circ$): three ($180^\circ$), four ($240^\circ$) or five ($300^\circ$) at a corner. Six already make $360^\circ$.
  4. Squares ($90^\circ$): only three ($270^\circ$). Pentagons ($108^\circ$): only three ($324^\circ$).
  5. Hexagons ($120^\circ$): three already make $360^\circ$. Polygons with even more corners have even bigger angles.

Exactly five possibilities remain. And for each of them there really is a solid.

EXAMPLE 1 · NO SOLID FROM HEXAGONS

Why is there no regular solid made of regular hexagons?

At least three hexagons would have to meet at a corner: $3 \cdot 120^\circ = 360^\circ$.

The hexagons lie flat like a honeycomb. No corner is formed.

EXAMPLE 2 · COUNTING CLEVERLY

The icosahedron has 20 triangles, and 5 meet at every corner. Calculate $k$ and $e$ without counting.

Together the triangles have $20 \cdot 3 = 60$ sides. Every edge belongs to two triangles: $k = 60 \div 2 = 30$.

Together the triangles have 60 corners, and 5 of them make up one corner of the solid: $e = 60 \div 5 = 12$

EXERCISES

Use the counting trick from Example 2 to calculate the edges and vertices of the tetrahedron and the octahedron.

Tetrahedron: $k = 4 \cdot 3 \div 2 = 6$, $e = 12 \div 3 = 4$. Octahedron: $k = 8 \cdot 3 \div 2 = 12$, $e = 24 \div 4 = 6$.

Which Platonic solids consist of triangles, which of squares, which of pentagons?

Triangles: tetrahedron, octahedron, icosahedron. Squares: cube. Pentagons: dodecahedron.

The dodecahedron has 12 pentagons, and 3 meet at every corner. Calculate $k$ and $e$.

$k = 12 \cdot 5 \div 2 = 30$, $e = 60 \div 3 = 20$

Draw a net of the octahedron made of equilateral triangles with side length 4 cm. Cut it out and build the model. Add glue tabs.

For example eight triangles in two rows: four triangles pointing alternately up and down in a strip, with two more attached above and two below. The 3D net in the book shows one possibility.

The interior angle of a regular heptagon is about $128.6^\circ$. Show that there is no regular solid made of heptagons.

At least three at a corner: $3 \cdot 128.6^\circ \approx 385.7^\circ > 360^\circ$. They overlap; a corner is impossible.

UNIT 24 LESSONS

2Euler’s polyhedron formula

There is a rule hidden in the counting table: cube $8 - 12 + 6 = 2$, square-based pyramid $5 - 8 + 5 = 2$, triangular prism $6 - 9 + 5 = 2$. The answer is always 2. The Swiss mathematician Leonhard Euler noticed this.

KEY POINT · EULER’S POLYHEDRON FORMULA

For every polyhedron without dents with $e$ vertices, $k$ edges and $f$ faces:

$e - k + f = 2$

If you know two of the three numbers, you can calculate the third: $\;f = 2 - e + k$, $\;e = 2 + k - f$, $\;k = e + f - 2$.

Leonhard Euler (1707 to 1783) from Basel worked in St Petersburg and Berlin. He wrote more than almost any other mathematician. He announced the polyhedron formula in 1750 in a letter to his friend Christian Goldbach.

INTERACTIVE · CHECK EULER ON MANY SOLIDS
EXAMPLE 3 · ONE NUMBER IS MISSING

A polyhedron has 12 vertices and 30 edges. How many faces does it have?

$f = 2 - e + k = 2 - 12 + 30 = 20$.

20 faces, for example the icosahedron.

EXAMPLE 4 · THE OCTAHEDRON IN OBLIQUE DRAWING

Draw an octahedron with edge length 4 cm as an oblique drawing.

The octahedron consists of two square-based pyramids, base to base. Draw the middle square as an oblique drawing: 4 cm at the front, 2 cm going backwards at $45^\circ$.

Above and below its centre put an apex at the same distance and join each to all four corners. The distance is about 2.8 cm (measured on the model).

EXERCISES

Check the polyhedron formula for the frustum of a pyramid, the pentagonal prism and the dodecahedron.

$8 - 12 + 6 = 2$, $\;10 - 15 + 7 = 2$, $\;20 - 30 + 12 = 2$

A polyhedron has 6 vertices and 12 edges. How many faces does it have? Which Platonic solid could it be?

$f = 2 - 6 + 12 = 8$: the octahedron.

A classic football is sewn from 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons. How many edges does it have? How many vertices? Check with Euler.

Sides: $12 \cdot 5 + 20 \cdot 6 = 180$; every seam belongs to two faces: $k = 90$. Three faces meet at every corner: $e = 180 \div 3 = 60$. Euler: $60 - 90 + 32 = 2$ ✓

Draw a cube with edge length 5 cm as an oblique drawing. Join four of its corners by face diagonals so that a tetrahedron is formed.

Choose one corner and the three corners diagonally opposite it on the neighbouring faces. The six face diagonals between them are the edges of the tetrahedron.

Justify the polyhedron formula for all prisms and all pyramids with an $n$-gon as their base.

Prism: $2n - 3n + (n + 2) = 2$. Pyramid: $(n + 1) - 2n + (n + 1) = 2$. The variable $n$ drops out each time.

TEST YOURSELF!

What is $e - k + f$ for the dodecahedron?

$20 - 30 + 12 = 2$

A polyhedron has 6 faces and 8 vertices. How many edges?

$k = 8 + 6 - 2 = 12$

How many edges does a prism with a heptagon as its base have?

$3 \cdot 7 = 21$

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

How many Platonic solids have triangular faces? Put them in order of the number of their faces.

Three: tetrahedron (4), octahedron (8), icosahedron (20).

Connecting with chapter 3.1: Draw a net of the tetrahedron with edge length 6 cm. Hint: a large equilateral triangle with side length 12 cm, divided through the midpoints of its sides.

The lines joining the midpoints of the sides divide the large triangle into four equilateral triangles with 6 cm sides. The three outer ones fold up and meet at the apex.

If you cut a small corner off every corner of a cube, you get a new solid. Count $e$, $k$ and $f$ and check Euler.

Every corner of the cube becomes 3 new vertices: $e = 24$. Edges: the 12 old ones and 3 new ones at each cut: $k = 36$. Faces: 6 and 8 new triangles: $f = 14$. $24 - 36 + 14 = 2$ ✓

Connecting with chapter 3.2: The centres of the six faces of a cube with edge length 6 cm form an octahedron. It consists of two square-based pyramids whose common base has an area of $18$ cm². Calculate the volume of the octahedron. What fraction of the cube is that?

Each pyramid is 3 cm high: $V = 2 \cdot \tfrac13 \cdot 18 \cdot 3 = 36$ cm³. The cube has 216 cm³, so the octahedron fills exactly $\tfrac16$ of it.

EXCURSIONHISTORY

Plato’s elements and Kepler’s cosmic mystery

The Greek philosopher Plato (around 428 to 348 BC) described in his work Timaeus what the world is made of. At that time people assumed four basic elements. Plato assigned a solid to each one: to fire the pointed tetrahedron, to earth the stable cube, to air the octahedron and to water the icosahedron. The dodecahedron was left over; he connected it with the universe as a whole. The five solids are called Platonic after him.

Almost 2000 years later, in 1596, the young Johannes Kepler published his book Mysterium Cosmographicum, “The Cosmic Mystery”, in Tübingen. Six planets were known at the time and so five gaps between their orbits, exactly as many as there are Platonic solids. Kepler nested the solids inside one another: the cube between Saturn and Jupiter, then the tetrahedron, dodecahedron, icosahedron and octahedron down to Mercury. Later, more accurate measurements showed that the model was wrong. Kepler himself held on to it to the end, but in searching for the plan he found the laws by which the planets really move.

Sources: Plato, Timaeus 53c–56c. J. Kepler, Mysterium Cosmographicum, Tübingen 1596. Euler to Goldbach, letter of 14 November 1750.

REGULAR POLYHEDRON

Equal regular polygons, the same number at every corner

Cube: 6 squares, 3 at each corner

EXACTLY FIVE

At least 3 faces per corner, together less than $360^\circ$

Triangles 3, 4, 5 · squares 3 · pentagons 3

COUNTING TRICK

Count all the sides of the faces and divide by 2 to get $k$

Icosahedron: $60 \div 2 = 30$

EULER

$e - k + f = 2$

$e = 12$, $k = 30$: $f = 20$
